description: We are building AstroCadet, an interactive web-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer powered by real NASA ISS telemetry and life-support data. Players master zero-gravity physics across three hands-on missions: 3D ISS docking, spacewalk oxygen/thermal management, and live orbital tracking. Led by an Aeronautical Engineering student, we are seeking Web/3D devs, UI/UX game designers, and storytellers to turn real spaceflight engineering into an accessible STEM game!
summary:
ASTRA JUNIOR – OUTPOST SURVIVAL is an interactive 3D space exploration and STEM learning game designed for children aged 7–12. It allows players to become junior astronauts and manage a research outpost on the Moon or Mars. Players make important decisions about life support, oxygen, water, food production, energy and radiation protection while responding to unexpected mission emergencies.

Through interactive environments, resource-management challenges and decision-based gameplay, children discover why every space mission requires careful planning and engineering trade-offs. Each decision has consequences, helping players understand how astronauts protect their crew and keep an outpost operating in extreme environments.

The project aims to make authentic space science more accessible, engaging and enjoyable for young learners by combining 3D exploration, educational explanations and space-survival gameplay.
details:
ASTRA JUNIOR: OUTPOST SURVIVAL

ASTRA JUNIOR – OUTPOST SURVIVAL is an interactive 3D educational game developed to introduce children aged 7–12 to the real challenges of human space exploration.

How it works:

Players take the role of a junior astronaut commander and choose between two destinations: the Moon and Mars. They must build and manage an outpost while keeping their astronauts safe and maintaining essential resources such as oxygen, water, food and power.

The game introduces resource-management decisions, including balancing energy use, maintaining life-support systems, growing food, protecting astronauts from radiation and responding to unexpected emergencies. Players learn that every decision has benefits and costs, and that poor resource planning can affect the survival of the mission.

Educational benefits and intended impact:

The project transforms complex space-engineering concepts into simple, interactive experiences. Instead of only reading facts about the Moon and Mars, children can explore environments, make decisions, observe consequences and learn from their mistakes. It encourages curiosity, scientific thinking, problem-solving, resource management and interest in STEM careers.

Technology and tools:

The project is developed as a browser-based application using JavaScript, React and Vite, with Three.js and React Three Fiber for interactive 3D environments. CSS is used for the interface and responsive design. The project is developed using Google Antigravity and deployed through Vercel. GitHub is used for source-code management if included in the actual development workflow.

Creativity and design considerations:

The project combines a space-adventure experience with simplified mission-management mechanics. It features interactive Moon and Mars environments, astronaut guidance, resource indicators, mission challenges and educational explanations. The design prioritises children aged 7–12 through simple language, visual feedback, accessible controls and engaging gameplay.

The project considers scientific accuracy, age-appropriate learning, accessibility, browser compatibility and the importance of distinguishing real NASA information from simplified game assumptions.

Overall goal:

To help children understand that space exploration is not only about reaching another planet, but also about making difficult engineering decisions to keep astronauts alive and missions successful.
